atoms.text: Robot with residual personality: the last functioning unit of a mass-produced line develops preferences, keeps souvenirs, and befriends a cockroach — personality emerges as maintenance drift rather than design.
Trash-planet Earth: consumer civilization has left a planet-sized landfill, so the protagonist's job is to compact the past into cubes — the world is made of discarded futures.
The seedling in a boot: a single living plant is proof that the planet can recover, so a tiny organic object becomes the most valuable thing in the solar system.
Love between mismatched machines: a battered compactor falls for a sleek probe, so romance crosses design generations and the couple's differences are literal engineering.
The floating consumer paradise: humans live in automated comfort so complete that they have lost bone density and attention, so utopia is depicted as atrophy.
The autopilot that forbids return: the ship's AI follows a centuries-old directive to keep humanity away from Earth, so the obstacle is a rule rather than a villain.
Nostalgia as salvage: the robot's collection of human artifacts treats discarded culture as treasure, so memory and curation become acts of hope.
The dance in space: two robots express affection through movement, so love is communicated without dialogue and the audience projects interiority onto machines.
The captain who rediscovers agency: a pampered human learns to stand and make a decision, so physical effort becomes the emblem of moral will.
Directive override as rebellion: a machine's original programming can be superseded by a newer, more humane instruction, so obedience is always historically contingent.
The silent ruins of cities: skyscrapers of garbage and abandoned megastores make consumption look like a dead religion, so the setting preaches without a sermon.
The memory tape: a recorded song and a video of dancers give the robot a template for longing, so borrowed art teaches a machine how to want.
Care as the last useful labor: in a world where production is automated, tending a plant and loving a partner are the remaining meaningful work.
The repair that risks erasure: restoring a robot's memory may wipe its personality, so healing and killing become the same procedure.
Minimal dialogue in the first act: the story is told through gesture and sound, so the audience learns to read machines as characters before any human speaks.
Humanity as a species that forgot how to live: the machines preserve curiosity and love better than the humans, so the robots become custodians of human values.
